As a twenty something trying to learn how to program his argument rings true to me in a certain sense. Starting out I would try to use online resources like Code Academy to get started. Code Academy is free and takes a very basic approach in trying to teach programming that often involves giving a one or two paragraph explanation of a concept and has the user simply fill in a small bit of code to complete the current exercise and move on to the next one. When you do this about ten times while having no background in coding you get the feeling that you are learning something, but later when you are tasked to build a functional project, like a simple card game which requires writing code from scratch and applying more difficult design methods, the task becomes much harder to complete and it's easy to get discouraged and not do it. This was my problem until I committed to wanting to learn to code and began taking college classes for programming that focused on teaching concepts in depth (and with rigor) at which point I began to actually learn to program and most importantly reached a breakthrough where I finally started to believe I could learn how to program even though I was starting in my mid-twenties.

How I think my experience learning to code relates to the argument of this TED talk is this: Code Academy is the brain child of some talented programmers who wanted to give people a quick and easily digestible way to get started programming. Their approach does just that, but in its current format only scrapes the upper most layer of the otherwise large challenges that come with trying to learn how to program. In a similar sense TED brings to the forefront interesting science, technology, and concepts to try and educate the general public and takes pride in doing so, but that education is a very brief and superficial one and fails to compel people to work for change. In the case of both Code Academy and TED they succeed more as a form of entertainment on the internet rather than as a channel to inspire personal growth and change. I personally think we are better off for having programs like TED or Code Academy rather than not having them, but it would be better if the format was tweaked somewhat to better educate and compel people to learn, grow, and seek to improve.

How should that be done? Don't know, and that's the weakest aspect of his talk. It is easy to criticize the current solutions in place than it is to build new ones, and being able to point out the problems is not nearly as valuable as being able to create new solutions for those problems to replace the old ones.
